Question three. What is amortized O of one, and when does it apply? It spreads a rare expensive step's cost over the cheap ones around it. Append a million items to a Python list. It runs out of room eighty-six times, and each move to a bigger block can copy every item so far. Add those copies up: about eight copies per append, at any length. Constant, on average. A textbook array doubles, for under two copies an append. Python grows by about an eighth, so it copies more often. Any fixed factor keeps it constant, a hash table's rehash too. But that's an average, not a promise per call: the append that triggers the last resize can copy nine hundred thirty-nine thousand items. On a latency budget, allocate up front.

Question four. When is a stack the right structure? When the problem is about the most recent thing still open: nesting, undo, backtracking. Last in, first out. A counter can't do it. This string opens and closes one round and one square bracket, so counting accepts it. But the round one closes while the square one inside is open. A stack keeps the openers, newest on top, and each closer must match the top: rejected. A queue matches the oldest opener instead, so it gets both wrong: it accepts this one, and rejects a correctly nested string. Depth-first search is the same idea: the path you're on is the stack.
